questions.q: Why are silent failures specifically dangerous in scheduled, unattended automation?
options: Nobody is watching the console when it runs, so without a durable log or an alert, a failure isn't noticed until its consequences surface later, often as a much worse problem
PowerShell scripts cannot fail when run on a schedule
Scheduled scripts automatically retry on failure, so silence is irrelevant
Silent failures only affect the log file, never the actual task
questions.explain: An interactive failure is seen immediately by the person running it; a scheduled failure with no record or alert can go unnoticed until, for example, a restore attempt finds nothing usable.

questions.q: What does the lesson's custom Write-Log function use to append entries to a log file?
options: Add-Content
Set-Content
Export-Csv
New-Item -Force
questions.explain: Add-Content appends a line without overwriting the file, which is exactly what a running log needs — Set-Content would overwrite the whole file each time.

questions.q: What does Get-DbatoolsLog retrieve, and how does it differ from a script's own custom log file?
options: It retrieves dbatools' own internal log of what its commands did internally, separate from whatever a script's own Write-Log function records about the script's decisions
It is the exact same thing as a custom Write-Log function, just a different name
It retrieves SQL Server's transaction log
It automatically emails the DBA team on every dbatools command run
questions.explain: Get-DbatoolsLog is dbatools' internal logging system for its own commands — a script's custom log records what the script itself decided to do, a different and complementary thing.

questions.q: What two things does this lesson add to Lesson 5's try/catch/finally pattern to make it automation-ready?
options: A durable, timestamped log file and an active alert (such as an email) so a failure doesn't sit unnoticed
A GUI popup and a sound alert
Removing the finally block since it's unnecessary in automation
Nothing — the pattern is identical, with no additions
questions.explain: The core addition is durability (a log file that persists after the run) and active notification (an alert someone actually sees), on top of the existing error handling.

questions.q: Per the lesson's example, why is $ErrorActionPreference = "Stop" set at the top of the automation-ready script?
options: It ensures errors from cmdlets are treated as terminating by default, so the try/catch actually catches them, consistent with Lesson 5
It disables all error handling for performance reasons
It has no effect and is left over from an older script version
It is required syntax for Add-Content to function
questions.explain: This directly reinforces Lesson 5's lesson about terminating vs. non-terminating errors — without it, the catch block might never fire.
